source.title: More is Better in Modern Machine Learning: when Infinite Overparameterization is Optimal and Overfitting is Obligatory
source.authors: James B. Simon; Dhruva Karkada; Nikhil Ghosh; Mikhail Belkin

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives results and reports experiments about random-feature and kernel regression that refine the scope of double descent: under fixed underregularization it shows a double-descent peak, while at optimally tuned ridge it proves test risk improves with more features and samples.
record.gate_note: Included the paper's own theoretical results and experimental outcomes on test risk, sample/feature scaling, ridge, and added label noise. Cited findings from other work are not rows. Exponent-estimation procedures and values used to fit theoretical curves are not outcomes on the claim.
record.test_reason: In RF regression and KRR, the paper's own theorems and experiments show a double-descent peak under weak ridge. They also prove that tuning ridge optimally removes the peak, so more features and more samples never hurt. This restates the scope of V3, V4 and V6. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in RF regression, with optimally tuned ridge, more features and more samples strictly help, so infinite width is optimal. For KRR on tasks with powerlaw eigenstructure meeting their exponent and noise condition, near-zero training error is obligatory for near-optimal test error. The tested image tasks with convolutional NTKs satisfy this condition, and added label noise moves the optimum away from interpolation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies random-feature regression and KRR with theoretical risk estimates and ridge sweeps, rather than reproducing deep-network size, epoch, or data sweeps from the cited double-descent sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Test-risk behavior depends on ridge choice: underregularized sweeps show a double-descent peak, while optimally tuned ridge yields monotonic improvement with more features or samples. Added label noise shifts the optimal fitting ratio away from zero.

fits_no_version.finding: In KRR with Myrtle CNTKs on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10 and FashionMNIST, the optimal fitting ratio is ≈0 without added noise. It becomes nonzero and grows as Gaussian label noise is added.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise shifts the optimal regularization away from interpolation in kernel regression on natural image tasks.

record.problems: The RF eigenframework derivation is described as nonrigorous and relies on a Gaussian universality ansatz. Experimental curve values are presented in figures without reported error bars in the text. The size/sample experiments concern RF or kernel regression, not trained deep networks or training epochs.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every ridge/noise curve in Figures 2 and 7: the text reports the aggregate noise-related change in optimal fitting ratio, while the plotted individual values are figure-only. Values for exponent estimates and values used to select or fit theoretical curves were excluded because they are not test-risk outcomes on the claim.

untested.parts: No deep networks trained end to end; only last-layer RF models and KRR.
Deep networks; only RF regression is shown.
Model classes other than RF and kernel regression.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise dependence of the peak height; triple or multiple descent.

missing.what: Theoretical result that at fixed ridge, bias strictly decreases with n and k, so any region of rising error (e.g. a double-descent peak) is attributable to variance.
Overregularized columns of Fig. 4: with large ridge the model does not interpolate and no diagonal peak is shown.

record.verdict_notes: Belkin is a coauthor, but this paper is not one of the original sources. The RF eigenframework is nonrigorous and rests on a Gaussian universality ansatz, so Theorems 1 and 2 are proved about the estimate, not the true risk. The double-descent evidence in experiments is figure-only and qualitative, with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: Model-wise double descent in deep networks.
The reported sample-size behavior is for random-feature regression, not deep networks generally; the paper also proves monotonic improvement when ridge is optimally tuned.
The tested model classes are random-feature regression and kernel ridge regression, not all model classes.
Whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
The study reports effects of added label noise on optimal fitting ratio and discusses optimally tuned ridge, but does not test multiple/triple descent or establish a variance-driven peak mechanism.
Whether an appropriate effective parameter count converts second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: RF regression
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 1 compares optimized test risk at different feature counts, with ridge minimized separately.

conditions.value: any task eigenstructure with nonzero learnable target component

rows.value: For k′ ≥ k, minδ′ Ete(n, k′, δ′) ≤ minδ Ete(n, k, δ), with strict inequality when k′ ≠ k and the target has nonzero learnable component.
rows.note: A theoretical monotonic improvement result under optimally chosen ridge, rather than a measured double-descent curve.
rows.check: Theorem 1 at optimal ridge says risk is monotone in k, so the peak disappears. This is what V6 states, so the row belongs to V6. Under V4 it would only read as an absent peak.

rows.subject: RF regression
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 1 compares optimized test risk at different sample counts, with ridge minimized separately.

conditions.value: any task eigenstructure with nonzero learnable target component

rows.value: For n′ ≥ n, minδ′ Ete(n′, k, δ′) ≤ minδ Ete(n, k, δ), with strict inequality when n′ ≠ n and the target has nonzero learnable component.
rows.note: In this tested setting, added samples do not raise optimized test risk; this does not rule out the claim's possibility under other regularization choices.
rows.check: Link and state are correct: at optimal ridge more samples strictly lower risk. It is also theoretical evidence for V6's regularization clause; the V6 verdict uses it via the text.

rows.subject: Synthetic Gaussian random-feature regression
rows.operation_detail: Varies the number of training samples n and plots train and test MSE across ridge settings.
rows.measure: Test MSE as sample size varies
rows.note: The text describes a signature double-descent peak in the underregularized setting and identifies the classical regime as to the right of the interpolation threshold; Figure 4 shows the n,k sweep.
rows.check: Figure-only and qualitative. The Fig. 4 caption names a 'signature double descent peak (bright diagonal)' in the underregularized n,k heatmap, so fixed-k sample sweeps rise near n≈k.

rows.note: The text explicitly describes a signature double-descent peak in the underregularized setting; Figure 1 also states that at optimal ridge more features monotonically improve test performance.

rows.subject: CIFAR10 random ReLU-feature regression
rows.operation_detail: Varies the number of random ReLU features k and plots test error at optimal ridge.
rows.measure: Test MSE as feature count varies
rows.note: The figure caption states that at optimal ridge, more features monotonically improve test performance.
rows.check: CIFAR10 random ReLU features at optimal ridge, with monotone improvement in k. This shows the peak vanishing under tuned regularization (V6), not the V4 double-descent shape.

rows.subject: RF regression
rows.size_stated: number of features k varied relative to n
rows.operation_detail: The zero-ridge Proposition 2 evaluates further increases in the larger of n and k after the double-descent peak.

conditions.value: k > n for increasing k; n > k for increasing n

rows.baseline: risk at the same ridge and smaller feature or sample count
rows.value: ∂Ete/∂k ≤ 0 when k > n; ∂Ete/∂n ≤ 0 when n > k
rows.note: The authors describe this as test performance improving after the double-descent peak.

rows.subject: KRR with Myrtle convolutional NTKs
rows.operation_detail: Varies ridge and added Gaussian label noise, measuring test MSE and optimal fitting ratio.

uncorrupted versus added label noise, including σrel² = 1, 5, and 50 in Figure 2

rows.check: Measures the optimal train/test fitting ratio in KRR as label noise is added, not a double-descent peak. It is a related construct, so it belongs in fits_no_version.
